Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Judge
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Breathing): Heavy breathing sounds, Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne, Tactile (Restrained): Feeling physically restrained or held down
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Vignette:
For as long as she could remember, Judge Abena Osei had prided herself on her clarity of mind. In the courtroom, she was known for her unflinching recall of precedent, her ability to hold complex arguments in her head like a carefully balanced scale. But that was before the basement. Before the three days in a windowless room in her home country, where the men who had once been her government’s security detail had decided she knew too much about a missing journalist. She had been a human rights lawyer then, not yet a judge. She had gone to meet a source, and instead, she had been taken.

What happened in that room was not something she could summon at will. When she tried, deliberately, to reconstruct the sequence—how they had first grabbed her arms, the sound of the metal door slamming, the particular cologne one of them wore, cloying and sweet—the memory would slip away like water through her fingers. She would find herself staring at the wall of her chambers, knowing she had been there, knowing it had happened to her, but the memory felt as though it belonged to a stranger. There were gaps, entire stretches of hours that she could not access. She knew, intellectually, that she had been interrogated, that she had been bound to a chair for nearly two days, that she had been deprived of sleep. But the details of those hours were simply gone, as if her mind had drawn a curtain across them and refused to pull it back.

The things that did return were not under her control. They came through her body, not her thoughts. The first time it happened after she had moved to the United States and taken her seat on the bench, she was in a pretrial hearing. The defense attorney, a heavyset man with a nervous habit, was standing at the podium, breathing heavily into the microphone. The sound—that rhythmic, humid rasp—hit her like a physical blow. For a moment, she was not in the courtroom. She was back in the chair, and one of the men was standing behind her, breathing close to her ear, whispering questions she could not answer. She gripped the edge of the bench and forced herself to breathe. No one noticed. She had learned to hide it well.

The olfactory triggers were worse. A thin woman in the jury pool wore a perfume that was almost identical to the cologne of the man who had held her down while another tied her wrists. Abena had to excuse herself for a recess, claiming a sudden headache. She sat in the bathroom stall, her hands shaking, certain that if she stayed in that room another minute, she would scream. She had come to believe that her body had its own memory, one that was more honest than her mind, and that it would betray her at any moment.

The most pervasive trigger was the feeling of being restrained. It was not that anyone was actually holding her down. It was the sensation of her own clothing, tight around her arms, or the way her husband would sometimes place a hand on her shoulder to wake her from a nightmare. She had stopped letting him touch her during the night. She slept on the far edge of the bed, rigid, her arms at her sides. She had also stopped wearing blazers with fitted sleeves. At work, she wore loose, flowing robes—judicial robes, which she had always found a comfort, now felt like a second skin that could not trap her.

Her avoidance had become a quiet architecture of her life. She no longer attended any social functions where people might embrace her. She had stopped going to the gym because the sight of someone using the leg press machine, strapped in, made her chest tighten. She told her husband she was too tired, and he believed her. He did not know about the basement. She had never told him. She had never told anyone. The memory felt so alien, so distant from the person she was now—a respected judge, a mother of two grown children, a woman who had built a life of order and fairness—that speaking it aloud would be like claiming a nightmare as her own biography.

She came to therapy because she had nearly lost her composure in open court last week. A defendant had been brought in wearing restraints, and the sound of the metal cuffs clicking had sent her into a dissociative state so profound that the bailiff had to call her name three times before she responded. She had adjourned early, citing illness. That night, she sat in her study and realized she could no longer trust herself to be the person the courtroom needed her to be. What frightened her most was not the memory itself, but the possibility that it would surface at the wrong moment and undo everything she had built. She hoped, more than anything, to find a way to make the memory feel like her own—to claim it, so that it would stop claiming her.
